title: Paired Household Tap-Water Sampling of Enterobacterales with Multidrug-Resistant Phenotypes in Al-Baha, Saudi Arabia
content: Background: Household tap water in bathroom and washbasin environments is an understudied reservoir of clinically significant and drug-resistant bacteria. Under-standing site-specific contamination patterns and their shared infrastructure-related predictors is critical for evidence-based interventions in community settings. This study investigated the prevalence, species distribution, and environmental risk factors for bacterial contamination — with particular emphasis on phenotypic multidrug non-susceptibility among selected isolates— in bathroom and washbasin tap water across residential households in the Al-Baha region, Saudi Arabia. Methods: A total of 278 samples were collected as a paired cross-sectional microbiological study across 139 households in Al-Mandaq, Al-Baha, and Bani Hasan governorates. Paired samples were collected simultaneously from bathroom and washbasin taps. MacConkey broth en-richment was followed by selective plating. Bacterial identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing were performed using the VITEK 2 automated system (bioMérieux, France). Paired analysis used McNemar's test, with site-specific multivariable risk factors identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Results: Presumptive culture-based contamination was detected in 19.4% (27/139) of bathroom taps and 18.7% (26/139) of washbasin taps. Simultaneous contamination at both sites occurred in 18 households (51% of all contaminated cases), with no statistically significant difference between sites (p=1.000). VITEK-confirmed isolates included Enterobacter cloacae, Citrobacter youngae, Citrobacter freundii, Citrobacter gillenii, Citrobacter werkmanii, and Pantoea agglomerans. Phenotypic multidrug non-susceptibility profiles were observed among the identified isolates. Iron tanks demonstrated a significant protective association against washbasin contamination (OR = 0.21; 95% CI: 0.05-0.85; p = 0.015). Concrete tanks and lower-level tank placement showed non-significant trends toward increased bathroom contamination risk. Conclusion: The paired contamination pattern suggests a possible shared house-hold-level water-system source from various factors , although this was not confirmed by direct tank/plumbing sampling or molecular typing. These findings support routine household water surveillance, improved tank maintenance, and further molecular and environmental studies to better understand antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in domestic tap-water systems.
